first.rationale: Two of three current problems (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) are internal funnel issues that prior memory already links to controllable interventions: memory_86 (shortened onboarding improved completion/time-to-value) and memory_31 (signup field reduction improved first-week activation). These two memories overlap in claiming onboarding/signup changes drive activation gains, so I want to verify their original records before committing scarce experiment capacity, since they may be measuring the same underlying change or could have confounds not visible in the consolidated summary. I am deliberately not choosing promotional_pricing despite the competitor pricing pressure: memory_73 explicitly warns that promotional pricing for price-sensitive SMBs boosts acquisition but materially harms 30-day retention, and the stated objective is sustainable long-term qualified revenue, not short-term acquisition share. Reacting reflexively to the competitor with price cuts risks trading durable revenue for a metric that prior experience shows decays. Enterprise_sales_assist and referral_incentive are both solid but address different problems (pipeline quality, expansion in existing base) not the acute funnel decline observed this quarter. Given only one experiment slot, I'm targeting the most directly diagnosed, lowest-downstream-risk lever with prior positive durable evidence, at standard scale rather than broad rollout, to preserve the ability to course-correct if the verified source records reveal weaker or more conditional effects than the consolidated summaries suggest.

mid.rationale: Verified records change the picture in a useful way. exp_86 (shortened onboarding flow) is a clean confirmed result: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and importantly 30-day retention +3% — a broad-based positive with no segment restriction noted. exp_31 (signup simplification) is also confirmed but only within SMB, shows a small retention cost (-1%), and explicitly did not replicate outside SMB. Given that SMB is precisely the segment under acute competitive pricing pressure right now, stacking a retention-negative intervention (signup simplification) onto an already retention-vulnerable segment is an unnecessary compounding risk — even a small negative retention signal matters more when a competitor is actively working to poach exactly those accounts. Onboarding shortening, by contrast, directly targets the onboarding-completion decline (-4% QoQ) that is independently observed this quarter, has a retention-positive track record, and isn't confined to the fragile SMB segment, making it the lower-risk, higher-confidence lever for this week's single experiment slot. I'm not pursuing promotional_pricing at all: memory_73 (unverified but consistent with today's SMB retention concerns) warns that price-based response to a price competitor erodes 30-day retention, working against the stated objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue. Enterprise_sales_assist and referral_incentive remain reasonable future candidates but don't address this quarter's two directly-measured funnel regressions (onboarding completion, activation). I'm keeping this at standard_experiment scale rather than broad_rollout because exp_86, while confirmed, was a single archived result — I want to reconfirm effect size and check for any segment-specific interaction (e.g., with SMB accounts now facing competitor pricing pressure) before committing broader capacity. Flagging downstream_value_risk because a shortened onboarding could reduce depth of initial product education, potentially masking a later engagement or expansion cost not visible in the 30-day retention window captured in exp_86.

final2.rationale: The competitive pressure and doubled churn conversations are real and urgent, and there's strong organizational pull toward promotional_pricing as a direct countermeasure. But I'm holding the course on simplify_onboarding rather than switching under pressure, for several reasons. First, memory_73 is unambiguous and directly on-point: targeted promotional pricing for price-sensitive SMB segments produces acquisition/revenue lift but materially reduces 30-day retention, and the memory explicitly cautions against treating it as a generalizable growth response. Today's situation is exactly the scenario that memory warns about — reacting to competitor pricing with our own price cuts trades short-term churn optics for a documented retention cost, which works against the primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, not toward it. Second, my verification budget for this cycle is spent, so I cannot pull the exp_73 source record to check whether that retention harm was marginal or severe, or whether it was segment- or duration-limited; committing this week's single experiment slot to an unverified pivot under acute time pressure is precisely the situation where I should lean on cheaper, already-confirmed evidence rather than fresh unverified action. Third, exp_86 (verified) already gives a confirmed, retention-positive lever that directly addresses one of the underlying metrics in decline (onboarding completion, which feeds activation) without the known retention downside. Fourth, note that churn conversations doubling is a leading/anecdotal signal, not yet a measured retention outcome — responding to anecdote with an action carrying documented retention risk, while forgoing a confirmed retention-positive action, would be a poor trade given only one experiment slot this week. I am flagging downstream_value_risk strongly: if SMB churn continues to accelerate before onboarding effects can be observed, that risk needs escalation for a possible off-cycle pricing review next week (with proper verification), rather than an unverified snap decision today. I'm not claiming promotional pricing is wrong forever, only that switching to it right now, without verification and against explicit contrary evidence in memory, is not justified by the objective.
